issues.legal_issue: A person against whom a court proposes to make a criminal complaint for an offence affecting the administration of justice has no right to be heard before the complaint is made.
material_facts: In a land-acquisition compensation proceeding, the court found that documents produced in evidence were fabricated and considered whether to refer the apparent offences for criminal inquiry.
The court ordered a complaint without first hearing the person accused of using the fabricated documents.
The accused challenged the order on the ground that he had been denied a hearing before the complaint was made.
issues.conclusion: The court was not required to hear the accused before making the complaint; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 340(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court decides whether an inquiry into an apparent offence connected with a court proceeding is expedient in the interests of justice. Section 341, which provides an appeal, does not create a right to be heard before the complaint is made. The person has a right to be heard in the magistrate’s pre-trial proceedings under Sections 238–240, including the opportunity to seek discharge. The court at the referral stage does not decide guilt. The Court relied on M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras, which cautions against expressing a view on guilt or innocence at that stage, and disagreed with the contrary approach in Nimmakayala Audi Narrayanamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh; it also noted M. Muthuswamy v. Special Police Establishment.

predicates.court_considers_referring_an_apparent_of: A court considers whether to refer an apparent offence for criminal inquiry.
predicates.alleged_offence_is_connected_to_a_court_: The apparent offence is alleged to have occurred in or in relation to a court proceeding, or to concern a document produced or given in evidence there.

issues.definition: When a court considers referring an apparent offence connected to its proceeding for criminal inquiry, the person accused need not be heard before referral.

issues.legal_issue: A preliminary inquiry before a court decides whether to make a criminal complaint is discretionary and is limited to deciding whether further inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice.
material_facts: After receiving information that documents used to support a compensation claim were forged, the court obtained and examined the relevant records and found the documents fabricated.
The court considered whether the apparent offences should be referred for criminal inquiry.
issues.conclusion: A preliminary inquiry is not mandatory; if conducted, it is for deciding whether further inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice, not whether a particular person is guilty.
issues.legal_principle: Section 340(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits a court to make a complaint after such preliminary inquiry, if any, as it thinks necessary. The inquiry is not a trial or a determination of anyone’s guilt; it assists the court in deciding whether an inquiry into the apparent offence is expedient in the interests of justice. Section 2(g) defines an inquiry as an inquiry other than a trial, and Section 195(1)(b) identifies the relevant category of offences. M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras supports the rule that the court should make no expression on guilt or innocence at this stage.

issues.definition: When a court considers referring an apparent offence connected to its proceeding for criminal inquiry, any preliminary inquiry is optional and serves only to assess whether further inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice.
